Immigration and punishment: open-ended answers from a survey experiment

Source: R/data.R
egami.Rd

Experiment 3 of Egami et al. (2022). Respondents on Amazon Mechanical Turk (September 2017) read about a 28-year-old man convicted of entering the United States illegally. In the treatment condition he had previously served two prison sentences, one for a violent crime, and had been deported; in the control condition he had never been imprisoned. Respondents said whether he should be sent to prison and explained what the US government should do and why. The answers are split into a training and a test half as in Egami et al.; the SAE and its labels were learned on the training half, the effects are estimated on the test half.

Usage

egami

Format

A list; the rows of data, E and activations are the same answers in the same order:

data

Data frame, 1,034 rows: doc_id, train (TRUE for the 521 answers of the training half), treat (1 = criminal history), prison (the closed-ended answer: "Yes", "No", "Don't know", or NA), text (the open-ended answer).

E

1,034 x 3,072 matrix: the answers' embeddings (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large), as returned by embed_texts().

W

3,072 x 7 matrix: decoder directions of a sparse autoencoder (M = 7, K = 2, seed 7) trained on the training half with train_sae().

labels

The seven directions' labels (gpt-4.1, label_features() on the training half).

fidelity

Data frame, 7 rows: feature, precision, recall, f1 of each label on training answers the labeller did not see.

activations

1,034 x 7 matrix: the SAE's activations of the answers.

Source

Egami, Fong, Grimmer, Roberts and Stewart (2022), "How to make causal inferences using texts", Science Advances 8. Replication data: Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/DVN/QHJN8V, CC0 1.0. Embeddings, SAE and labels: Wirsching (2026). Built by data-raw/egami.R.
